To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the age-related loss of muscle mass and strength is progressive, 2) muscle strength at T 1 is a major predictor of strength at T 2, 3) muscle CSA is a strong predictor of muscle strength at T2, and 4) the age-related decline in muscle CSA is due, in part, to a decrease in the percentage of muscle fiber cross-sectional area that is type I.

12 yr of aging in sedentary men results in a 20-30% loss of muscle strength at the knee and elbow and that the cross-sectional area of skeletal muscle, as measured by computerized tomography, is a major contributor in this decline.
the loss in muscle strength with advancing age can be attributed, to a large extent, to a reduction in muscle CSA.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of age-related changes in the human skeletal muscle.
age-related changes in muscle size and function.
the effects of aging on skeletal muscle structure and function and the relationship between these parameters.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the aging of muscle involves a loss of muscle CSA, a reduction in type I fibers, a loss of capillaries, and a decrease in muscle strength.
, as we age, our muscle fibers decrease in size and number and become weaker.
the aging muscle undergoes a process that is characterized by loss of muscle mass and strength, with a reduction of the proportion of type I muscle fibers and a decrease in capillary-to-fibre ratio.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the loss in muscle CSA and strength is not a function of the loss of muscle fibers but rather of a decrease in fiber size.
the loss in skeletal muscle mass with age is a major contributor of the loss in muscle strength.
the age-related loss of muscle mass is a primary determinant of the loss of muscle strength in the elderly.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the loss of muscle size is the primary contributor to age-related loss of muscle strength, and that the loss of capillary density is an important component of the loss of muscle CSA.
muscle strength in the elderly can be predicted with a high degree of accuracy by the combination of muscle strength and size at baseline and change in size between baseline and 12-yr follow-up.
the loss of muscle mass is the major contributor to the age-associated decline in strength.
